title: Testing Continuity at a Piece Boundary
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: For $h(x)=2x$ ($x\le 1$), $h(x)=3-x$ ($1<x\le 3$), $h(x)=0$ ($x>3$), decide whether $h$ is continuous at $x=1$ by comparing the two one-sided behaviors with the function value.
finalAnswer: h \text{ is continuous at } x=1 \text{ since } \lim_{x\to 1^-}h=\lim_{x\to 1^+}h=h(1)=2

steps.title: Approach from the Left
steps.explanation: For $x<1$ the active rule is $2x$, whose limit as $x$ climbs to $1$ is $2$.
steps.why: Left-hand limits use only the formula governing inputs below the boundary.

steps.title: Approach from the Right
steps.explanation: Just above $1$ the rule $3-x$ applies and also tends to $2$.
steps.why: Right-hand limits use the formula valid strictly above the boundary.

steps.title: Compare with the Function Value
steps.explanation: The boundary point belongs to the first branch and $h(1)=2$, matching both one-sided limits.
steps.why: Continuity requires the value and both limits to coincide.

steps.title: Conclude No Jump
steps.explanation: Since left limit, right limit, and function value all equal $2$, $h$ is continuous at $x=1$; the two pieces genuinely meet there.
steps.why: The three-way equality is precisely the definition of continuity at a point.
